newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: FEATURE-Cricket an escape for Sri Lankans weary of war.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Cricket an escape for Sri Lankans weary of war.

text.p: Sri Lankans, frustrated by a 13-year ethnic war that has claimed tens of thousands of lives, have found something to cheer them -- cricket.
Traffic thins on usually crowded streets, trading stalls at the stock exchange, and offices around the country are deserted when the Sri Lankan cricket team takes the field.
When a match is on few people think of the war and heroics on the cricket field matter more than those on the battlefield.
"There is something to look forward to (in cricket). With this war there are very few things to look forward to," said Vasi Nessiah, a computer executive.
Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) rebels are fighting for an independent homeland for minority Tamils in the north and east of this mainly Sinhalese island in the Indian Ocean.
The government says more than 50,000 people have died in the war. The LTTE says the toll is higher.
CRICKET BRINGS OUT SRI LANKAN PRIDE
Thousands of cheering fans waited in blistering heat to welcome the country's cricketers led by captain Arjuna Rantunga on their return from winning the World Cup in Pakistan last year.
A winning streak for the team in limited-overs cricket has sustained the feeling of national pride in this small, poor nation at the foot of India.
Every win brings war-weary fans out onto the streets and at cocktails, weddings, in offices and at home they spend hours discussing the merits of the game and the players.
But while they like their cricketers to win, Sri Lankans are also ready to forgive them when they lose.
A disastrous tour of New Zealand earlier this year did little to affect Sri Lankan enthusiasm. Later victories at Sharjah and then in India wiped out the bad memories.
"Sustained losing will affect the morale of the country. But whenever they lose there is this feeling that they will bounce back," said Nessiah.
CRICKET FEVER ALL AROUND
The cricket team's overseas exploits have resulted in Sri Lankans spending even more time in front of their television sets.
During the recent Independence Cup tournament in neighbouring India, drowsy Sri Lankans stumbled into offices each morning after staying up late to watch the live matches.
The state-owned Rupavahini Corporation came in for severe criticism when it decided not to telecast live a crucial semi-final match between India and Pakistan.
Still, when a recording of the match was televised the next day, most Sri Lankans stayed home glued to their sets.
The team's Australian coach Bruce Yardley is amazed by the cricket fever.

"You see the kids on the street learing the skills. They are copying their heroes. It's difficult to put a finger on one thing, but I think it's just the joy they feel in playing cricket that makes them so good," he told Reuters.
"The people here have a will to succeed in cricket."
CRICKETERS ARE MEDIA DARLINGS
The cricket madness has made television icons of the country's players, whose success has not been lost on profit-minded advertisers.
Companies are increasingly soliciting cricketers to advertise their products to Sri Lanka's younger generation, which idolises the sport stars.

The face of big-hitting batsman Sanath Jayasuriya, who dispatched opposition bowlers all over the ground in the World Cup, crops up constantly on television, endorsing consumer electronics, a bank and even powdered milk, while strike bowler Chaminda Vaas has become pitch man for a local brand of soft drinks.
